title: For people who made a game using AI, how much of your code do you understand?
author: drinkingnoodles
selftext:
I want to get a general idea of the percentage of people who have built a game from start to finish,   
  
which category do you fit in?  
  
1. full understanding of each function in their code

2. have knowledge of the overall structure of what each piece of code does

3. don't have any clue what their code does

if you fit in any of these categories, why?

For example,  
  
if you fit in category 1-2, maybe you enjoy coding here and there, so you like understanding how your game works from the inside.

If 3, is it perhaps because you see no difference in the result of the game experience and the end result, and have no intention to care about the nuances in your code?

comments.author: AnythingButUseful
comments.body:
I’d probably put myself in category 2. I don’t think you need to understand every single line to be able to build a game effectively, especially when AI is doing a lot of the implementation. But I do think you should understand the overall architecture and be able to explain what the important systems are doing.

For me, the line is debugging. If something breaks and you have absolutely no idea where to look or what the code is supposed to do, you’re basically dependent on the AI to fix its own mistakes. 😂 AI is great at writing code, but I still want enough understanding to actually own what I’ve built.

comments.author: Schwolop
comments.body: Somewhere between 2&3. I’m sure I could get to understand it, but … why? I don’t need to. I explain the bugs I observe, my hypothesis, ask for candidate explanations, suggest instrumentation that would narrow it down, review proposed fixes, interrogate how the fix will impact other systems, and so on. Why do I need to inspect the assembly language when I’ve learnt to trust the compiler? Wait, sorry, we’re one step up the abstraction tree: why do I need to read the code when I’ve learnt to trust the coding agent?

replies.author: outdatedhuman
replies.body:
Mostly because you won't know if your systems are doing what they are supposed to. You are squashing bugs, but the bugs you are squashing are the ones that are visible/obvious. There could be a lot more bugs that present themselves only in edge cases, or are just slightly off that you won't notice right away but are impacting the game feel holistically. That could be animations slightly off, damage calculation slightly wrong, modifiers not being applied, deadlocked quests, spawn rate, etc.

The second reason, at least for me, is to better guide further development, as code gets added in such a fast pace, it is easy to get out of touch with the system you are building and not able to make the best decisions at every turn. As it gets close to release, you might wanna tune in performance and polish the game, that's when you find out that the whole code base turned into a mess and every change just adds to the pile, and you are left with that feeling f* should I just refactor the whole thing.

The compiler example doesn't really apply. You learned to trust the compiler because it gives you the same result everytime you compile the same code, it was written and perfected across decades of software engineering by very smart people and tested to oblivion. AI is the exact opposite of that, and it is known and accepted by the software engineering industry that you shouldn't trust AI. This is not an anti-ai statement, it's just how the technology works.

replies.author: RecursiveServitor
replies.body:
> AI is the exact opposite of that, and it is known and accepted by the software engineering industry that you shouldn't trust AI.

It's not binary though. I trust GPT to write sensible code for my game given the architecture and direction I provide. And when it does do something suboptimal I trust it to fix that. 

I wouldn't trust it with my life however.

replies.author: outdatedhuman
replies.body:
Yeah, I agree, it's risk assessment at the end of the day.

The thing is you can't trust GPT to write sensible code all the time because it won't, and similarly you shouldn't expect it to fix things it doesn't know is wrong.

So if you trust these two premises, it is certain that given enough time the code will deviate from what you originally envisioned, and you will have no idea about it, GPT will have no idea about it. There will just be the code, the limited GPT context window and yourself, as 3 separate entities.

The risk assessment point means that for most of the ppl here who are playing game dev, and won't ever ship a game or if shipped won't do great, that was never a risk. But if you are quitting your job to go full indie, then that's when it matters that you design the game yourself and that you verify the AI code actually does what you designed it to.

replies.author: RecursiveServitor
replies.body:
With enough iteration it absolutely will catch mistakes. Especially because what I care about is the overall architecture. It's not going to consistently hallucinate that two systems are properly separated if they are really deeply entangled.  And in gamedev deep code issues tend to surface as either bad perf or obviously wrong behavior. I've already had it run debugging for single digit FPS. Stuff like that happens and it's often a simple fix. 

It can also generate screenshots which it can reason about visually. It came up with this autonomously.

replies.author: outdatedhuman
replies.body:
It absolutely won't, the big techs that laid off thousand of employees are just rehiring them now because AI on its own fails at complex task and quality control. I've seen it multiple times with frontier models across different non-game projects, but that's not even the issue I'm pointing at.

Hallucinations, code that wont compile, crashes, those are all easy to spot and easily fixable.  

The bugs Im talking about are the ones that you don't notice play testing it, and thus won't ask the AI to fix it. They will ship to production, you will play the game, it will feel slightly off and you won't know why.

Maybe our disagreement is at scale and complexity of the game, and for your use case it works wonders... It is just that game feel and fun is really hard to design/tune/code. Everyone can make a game, few can make a fun game, that's where I'm coming from, if you let AI do the whole work you will end up with a median of all the games it's trained on, while, the thing that made each of these games fun is the actual deviation from de median.

replies.author: RecursiveServitor
replies.body:
Making architectural decisions, project direction, spec work. And playtesting, of course. You need a human to judge game feel.

I'm also having it do FP with immutable records, because constraining mutation is exceptionally helpful to LLMs.

Like you, I'm a professional SWE. I think "vibecoding" is too broad for what we can do with AI. We aren't just YOLOing. I understand the entire stack and can, hypothetically, read the code and understand what each piece is doing. Even if I don't regularly do that it still means I have a mental model of what can possibly be happening when there's an issue. 

>The cause of layoffs is up for debate, but my point stands that AI output has quality issues and having AI running the shop didn't work.

It's also just severely out of date.

[https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2024/01/10/duolingo-ai-layoffs/](https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2024/01/10/duolingo-ai-layoffs/)

They started this supposed AI replacement in 2023.

>Do this then, paste this whole discussion in a LLM and see which points holds and which points are weak.

Ok.

>Since you explicitly suggested asking an LLM: your strongest point is the one about latent semantic bugs. RecursiveServitor is overstating things if they say enough iteration will *necessarily* find them. It won’t.  
  
But I think you’re also assuming that meaningful human oversight means manually reviewing the generated implementation. That’s the actual disagreement. In this project \[mine\], the human is defining architecture, mechanics, UX, specifications and acceptance criteria, then testing the resulting behavior and deciding when the implementation or architecture needs to change. The AI is doing most of the implementation and a lot of the inspection/debugging.  
  
That workflow can absolutely produce undetected errors. The interesting question is whether its verification mechanisms make those errors acceptably rare—not whether AI output is intrinsically trustworthy. Human-written software ships subtle bugs too.  
  
And “companies tried letting AI run the shop and rehired people” is weak evidence for this particular claim. Even where that description is accurate, it concerns different tasks, workflows, models and substantially older capabilities. It certainly establishes that “replace the engineering organization with an LLM” was a bad idea. Nobody here is proposing that.   
  
So I think you’ve identified a genuine risk, but you keep turning it into a stronger claim than the argument supports.

replies.author: outdatedhuman
replies.body:
Hey, didn't see your message yesterday.

Yeah I agree with you, there is a balance to it and it is up to everyone to decide how they work. I realized I was pushing my dev work process onto others, I guess I got triggered by the compiler comparison on the first comment as that was outrageous.

That said, I still defend that you gotta know and verify how at least the systems/mechanics are implemented in your game, because it is really easy for someone to miss a spec, and the AI silently filling the blank, or for the AI to make mistakes, sometimes really dumb mistakes, like you ask it to add something, it does but it also removes something somewhere else that had nothing to do with it, maybe it's a part of the game that you already tested, that now behaves differently. 

Anyways, having worked so much with coding agents, and also fixing other devs vibe code on critical projects where a bug can crash hundreds of thousands of machines, I've lost track of how many times I had to slap the agent, like what the f are you doing, bro? I understand that these are high risk projects thus more scrutiny is required, but this experience also showed me you just can't trust AI. It's a really good tool, I love it, but it is still a next-token predictor, it ain't smart and it can't really reason, it lacks intentionality, awereness and a true view of the world. It can't tell if it's wrong or not, it needs us to do all these things for them.

So I have this ingrained feeling, that if you don't check what the code is doing, given enough iterations, the code will deviate from the original design, maybe it will do less, maybe more, maybe be wrong. Add that to how tight and precise the code needs to be to deliver a fun game experience, I can't help to think that if you are not on top of things, you are leaving it to luck whether the game will be fun or not, you can have the same game, same mechanics with slightly different implementations,, 1 version of it is fun while 99 versions aren't.

Regarding the layoffs, I know it was a play by the boards to increase the profit for the year, they knew AI couldn't replace all those people. But that doesn't change the fact  AI can't replace people, if it could they would def not rehire people and keep the higher profit margins even if quality went a bit down. The fact that they didn't means it's not a slightly less quality problem, more of a they can't delivery their services/products.

comments.author: One_Salty_Pigeon
comments.body:
I'm somewhere between 2 and 3.  
  
I have a background in Software Development and QA / Automated testing and have dabbled in game development in the past but the current game I'm making I have almost no understanding of the code base and truthfully it's going ALOT smoother then you'd expect. Granted I've ran into plenty of bugs but being good at testing and explaining very clearly how a bug is occurring to GPT and Claude has solved all of my problems. 

But I think that's where having my background helps and makes AI code development easier. I know how to test, I understand how code works, and I understand how to explain in painful detail the exact steps, scenario, and likely causes of a bug with out even seeing the code in 99.9% of the cases.

I also think it helps though that the game I'm developing is a shop sim game so the overall code is not extreme physics or math and likely rather straight forward for the most part. That's my experience so far at least.

replies.author: R3DB71ND
replies.body:
It really does help to have a programming background. I use Claude Code and while it's very good, once the code base starts getting very large it will start to slop. I caught it being super inefficient with debugging and testing, so I helped it develop a debug mode to test even faster. It would not have done so by itself.

It will also start to repeat code in different classes and bloat up controllers. I noticed it taking longer and longer to do things, so I had it refactor by abstracting classes and using an event bus system. This ended up making Claude faster and not waste tokens. Again, it would have kept going down a certain path without my intervention.

replies.author: One_Salty_Pigeon
replies.body:
That and tying it to a design system seems to help but you have to regularly remind it and double check it's work even then sometimes. I've noticed when I'm patient and have it work on small changes ticket by ticket it tends to be ALOT better about avoiding bugs and creating massive piles of useless code or dead code even. 

But having clean code makes a huge difference. At my full time job I had the ability to rewrite our automated testing framework recently and it's crazy how clean code has just made everything with AI 1000 times better from it's ability to understand things to creating new code, I mean giving it a template to follow when possible to is another trick I've learned in bigger application builds. 

But having this background make such a big difference even when prompting because instead of saying "my parking lot system is broke" I can say things like "I think after the car leaves the parking lot it's not releasing it's reserved spot can you verify this by hooking into unitys CLI and watching what's happening" etc etc.

I am already architecturally designing constraints and structures in which the AI should build. I build these beforehand so that it knows that I expect expansion and variability in certain areas, to make certain parts of code repeatable, which parts of code need to take in a parameter so that it can use the same logic for multiple events occurring. I am already spending the effort structuring these logic branches and trees so I won’t be surprised in the future by something not being scalable.

I am essentially project manager. I don’t need to be project manager AND micro manage my engineer, bc that is very inefficient and you will get nothing done that way.

Sorry, I don’t meet that purity test. But I’m still going to do my best to release a polished product.

comments.author: CharlestonChewbacca
comments.body:
I've been a professional SWE of one form or another for nearly 2 decades and have been making games since I was about 8 years old, tinkering around on my Commodore. 

I would say 2. I don't need to know every line. Even when I was manually writing code, I didn't know every line. Anyone who answers 1 is either working on a very small project, they're lying, or they've dedicated every second of their life to what they're doing. 

Engineers think in systems. When we were manually programming, sure, we were writing one line at a time, but that was to build one component at a time. When you finish a component, you're not thinking about specific lines and functions too much anymore. You're thinking about systems and how all the components interact.

When I use AI to assist my coding, I'm still thinking about systems and how the components interact, I'm just largely not thinking about individual lines anymore. 

If it's a super critical function that's going to be used everywhere, sure, I'll read the code and think about ways it can be more efficient, or more modular/compatible/reusable, or more specific/general as necessary. But the majority of the code in any codebase is really just a commodity at this point.

My 3D engine has 300k+ Rust LoC, 20k+ wsgl LoC and I barely ever look at the detail. Yet it is architected as modular/plugin-based from the get-go. I want to understand how exactly it calls the wgpu api? I know which module to look at. I want to understand how the render pipeline works? Sure i can go in that other module. I want to check the finer details of how the shark meshes and animations are procedurally executed? No problem i go into the shark.rs file and take it from there. Do i think the code is a 100% neat? No I don’t. Because when Fable 5.5 is out, and then 6, and then 7 and so on, I can get it to refactor and clean it up.

I’m too busy directing the building of the next feature to spend too much time checking the engine room in detail.

comments.author: TheReviewerWildTake
comments.body:
Striving to keep it close to 1.   
  
But it depends - there is a code that is important to understand just to know whether you can easily change something, whether new feature will require a lot of sketchy rewrites and refactoring or just needs one extra class, whether your foundation is even fit to be scaled in certain way etc.  
Making an educated guess where to look for an issue, or how to limit AI scope so, that it does not break anything accidentally  - also requires understanding of code and programming practices, otherwise you just prompt and pray, which will eventually starting to fail you.  
   
And then there are libraries that do some dirty work, that take input X and give output Y -  and usually in soft. development you just make sure that they are safe, up to date, don\`t use anything deprecated and do what they promise, but typically you don\`t have time to study every single plugin line by line, and have no time to reinvent those.   
As long as you understand where it has to sit and what are the inputs and outputs, it is fine.  
But this part usually stays as number 2.  


I tried vibecoding before, and it ended up as one big demoralizing mess, because when you are looking at that huge project that still requires a lot of work and polishing - it feels so alien, as if you don\`t even belong there, and learning it takes a lot more time, compared to if you observed it grow class by class, method by method.   
Plus , changing or fixing that mess is unreliable and scary. God forbid if someone asks whether you can do X, Y, Z and "how long it might take" ... yeah, brb and lemme just ask Claude :D   
Nah, from my experience, №3 sucks for anything mildly ambitious, unless it is something like "build and forget".

comments.author: ThreeDMK
comments.body:
Depends on the systems:

Client/server: 1  
Tools: 1  
Work in blender: 1 to 2  
This new DAW Claude built for me yesterday?  3

I have worked or supported all of these things in some capacity.  I also have 10+ years working in the games industry supporting client/server integrations as well as architecting cloud solution for platform services.  Account, entitlements, micro transactions, security.  Have also been through launch events and seen what 1m people can do your stack.  

AI makes it easier to dive into some of these unknown areas and feel more comfortable.  My current generative audio work is a huge unknown for me.  The tool I built has been created in a way that exposes more details so that it’s not only a generation tool, but also a learning experience.  Seeing how audio voices are built/shaped is fascinating.  As I dig in I learn more.  If things don’t make sense I dig in until they do.

I have read less than 5% of the code that it builds for me, but I also have strict code standards and validation in place from nearly a year of development on my personal harness.  I can see when things drift now, usually any time I switch to newer models.  Every time I check source things are still being written the same way; standards are being followed, naming conventions adhered to.  I stopped really worrying about code quality a while ago.  :)
